newsitem.title: CHINA: Asian currency blight unsettles Hong Kong.
newsitem.headline: Asian currency blight unsettles Hong Kong.

text.p: Persistent contagion throughout Southeast Asian currency markets unsettled the Hong Kong dollar on Monday but most analysts still knocked down any suggestion of speculative weakness.
"I don't think the Hong Kong dollar is likely to fall prey to speculators," said Dong Tao, economist at Schroder Securities in Hong Kong.

Short-term interest rates soared and currency forwards widened in Hong Kong after speculators attacked the Indonesian rupiah, a currency that had seemed immune to speculation swirling through the region this month.

As heavy speculative selling pushed the rupiah to a new record low of 2,655 to the U.S. dollar, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority, the territory's de facto central bank, intervened to support the Hong Kong dollar spot rate.

The intervention lifted the Hong Kong dollar within a safe distance of the key psychological level of HK$7.7500. At 0500 GMT, the Hong Kong dollar was back on firmer ground, trading at HK$7.7470/80 and well-linked to its 14-year-old fixed rate of HK$7.80 to the U.S. dollar.
Traders said any break of the HK$7.7500 level could signal a sharp slide, which was why the HKMA was determined to defend it.
But traders were tense.
"Everyone is nervous," one dealer said. "Yes, definitely, everyone is nervous."
Speculators have already forced a depreciation of the Thai baht and Philippine peso, and currencies are jittery in Malaysia and even Singapore, long considered a safe haven.

The Malaysian ringgit was still weak on Monday after hitting a 38-month low in London on Friday, while the Philippines central bank was forced to intervene yet again to support its battered peso on Monday, which was trading at 28.35 to the U.S. dollar compared with pre-July 11 depreciation levels of 26.
The Thai baht, now trading at about 30.35 to the U.S. dollar compared to pre-July 2 depreciation level of 25, was sluggish with most of the domestic market on holiday.
In Hong Kong, currency forwards widened to 210 in the three-month and 400 in the six-month from more usual levels in the single digits, and money market rates soared.
The overnight rate climbed to 6.37 percent, while the one-week Exchange Fund bill yield reached 6.53 percent compared with 5.31 percent last week.
Spreads to corresponding U.S. government paper widened sharply.
Despite the tension, analysts remained confident that the Hong Kong dollar would remain an island of stability in a sea of currency turmoil.
"Hong Kong's fundamentals are much stronger than many of the Southeast Asian economies. Hong Kong's foreign exchange reserves are huge even without added support from China," Tao said.
Hong Kong holds at least US$63 billion in foreign exchange reserves while China, which has promised to defend the Hong Kong dollar if it comes under attack, has a cache of US$121 billion.
HKMA chief executive Joseph Yam has issued repeated warnings to speculators never to attack the Hong Kong dollar.

The territory's vast reserves and strong economic fundamentals set Hong Kong apart from some of the most troubled Asian nations now battling currency speculators, as does Yam's market credibility and that of the institution he controls.
But confidence is key in this situation and, following weakness in the Singapore dollar, there are signs of eroding confidence in Hong Kong.

"I think (Yam's) message has been heard but because of the hectic happenings in the regional currency markets investors might be just too nervous to take notice of what Mr. Yam has to say," the dealer said.
